Trump wants fewer Indian technology professionals moving to America. The unintended consequence may be more American technology work moving to India.

I have spent more than three decades in this industry. So when I read about the latest US action restricting some large technology companies from using PERM, the route through which employees move towards permanent residency, I was less worried than the headlines suggested.

One number explains why. Indian IT companies accounted for less than 1,400 of the 117,849 PERM certifications last year. Less than 2%. The direct impact may therefore be smaller than it first appears.

But something more interesting is happening underneath.

The original Indian IT model was simple. The customer had important work in America, so we sent Indian engineers there to do it. Then we discovered that much of that work could be done from India. The onsite-offshore model was born. I lived that transition.

We may be at the beginning of another one.

America is making it harder to move Indian talent there, while technology is making it easier for smaller teams in India to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated work.

There is an irony here. In trying to reduce the movement of Indian talent to America, the US may accelerate the movement of American work to India.

But I don’t mean another wave of coding and maintenance jobs.

The opportunity is architecture, product engineering, cybersecurity, AI implementation, industry solutions and eventually ownership of products and IP.

Indian teams should not merely receive specifications from New York. They should help decide what gets built. Not merely maintain a global bank’s technology platform, but help redesign the bank. Not just supply engineers to solve somebody else’s problem, but own the problem.

There is an uncomfortable truth too.

For thirty years, growth in Indian IT and growth in Indian IT employment travelled together. Win more business, hire more engineers.

As AI technology improves productivity, that relationship may weaken. Indian IT could win more sophisticated work and create more value without headcount growing at the same rate.

So we need a different definition of success.

For thirty years, Indian IT competed largely on the cost of Indian talent. The next thirty will depend on the capability of Indian talent.

Can we create architects rather than only programmers? Build products and IP here? Move more global decision-making to India? Create more value per person and therefore pay our people far better?

Those are much bigger questions than how many visas America issues.

So worry not about the visa headlines.

Trump may make it harder for Indian engineers to move to American work. The opportunity is to make American work move to Indian engineers.

It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts. Congresswoman Omar came to this country with her father when she was 12 years old. Five years later, her father became a naturalized citizen. If Ilhan had been 18 at the time, she would have had to apply for citizenship separately. But because she was 17, she became a naturalized citizen automatically.

Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress. There, she has been one of the Trump Administration’s fiercest critics, which has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country.

Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.

Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it’s not the first time this has happened. Under President Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly gone after those he considers his political enemies — from the Attorney General of New York, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve.

In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota.

The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.

We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. 🪔 Diwali picks for 2026: 
Instead of 10-15, I have come out with "20 Small & Midcap Stocks From Leading Brokerages Worth Tracking"

As I mentioned that I was going through Diwali stock recommendations from leading brokerage houses & after reviewing recommendations from over 20 brokerages, including Motilal Oswal, JM Financial, Mirae Asset Sharekhan, SBI Securities, Arihant Capital, Monarch, Choice International and Equirus, I have narrowed down my initial list.

Most of the frequently recommended companies were largecaps. Nothing wrong with them, but my interest has always been more towards smaller businesses where earnings can grow much faster than the broader market. Particularly those where a 20–30% annual earnings growth, combined with reasonable valuations, can lead to disproportionate returns over 3–4 years.
For this exercise, I have kept the market capitalisation between ₹5,000 crore and ₹50,000 crore.
Here are the 20 names that made my initial shortlist.

20 Small & Midcap Stocks

1. Navin Fluorine (Mirae Asset Sharekhan, Shriram)

MCap: ~₹42,400 Cr

Specialty fluorochemicals and CDMO business. New capacities and higher-value products could improve profitability considerably. The growth opportunity is attractive, although much of the optimism is already reflected in valuations.

2. Blue Star (Monarch, Choice International)

MCap: ~₹32,500 Cr

India's room AC penetration remains relatively low. Blue Star has a strong position in cooling and commercial refrigeration. Capacity expansion and a growing distribution network could support earnings for several years.

3. Syrma SGS Technology (PL Capital)

MCap: ~₹28,100 Cr

Electronics manufacturing with exposure to industrial, automotive and consumer segments. Revenue growth is encouraging, but the more interesting opportunity lies in improving operating margins as the business scales.

4. Sansera Engineering (KC Securities)

MCap: ~₹25,700 Cr

Known for precision automotive components, but the expansion into aerospace, defence and other non-auto businesses could change its earnings profile over time. A business worth watching beyond the automobile cycle.

5. HBL Engineering (PL Capital)

MCap: ~₹23,300 Cr

One of the interesting companies in railway safety systems, particularly Kavach. The opportunity is sizeable, but orders need to translate into actual earnings and cash. The valuation also leaves limited room for disappointment.

6. Jyoti CNC Automation (SBI Securities)

MCap: ~₹23,200 Cr

India's growing investment in manufacturing and precision engineering works in its favour. SBI Securities expects around 34% PAT CAGR during FY26–FY28. A strong growth assumption, so execution will matter more than the narrative.

7. Lumax Auto Technologies (Mirae Asset Sharekhan, Choice International)

MCap: ~₹15,900 Cr

Increasing component content per vehicle, premiumisation and acquisitions are changing the scale of this business. If acquired businesses integrate well and margins improve, earnings could grow faster than revenue.

8. Shaily Engineering Plastics (Motilal Oswal)

MCap: ~₹14,000 Cr

Moving deeper into pharmaceutical drug delivery devices, particularly injection pens. Motilal Oswal expects around 48% annual PAT growth through FY28. The key question is how quickly the new customer programmes scale and how much is already priced in.

9. CCL Products (Monarch)

MCap: ~₹12,900 Cr

An established instant coffee exporter with a growing branded business. Higher capacity utilisation and expansion into value-added products could lift profitability. Coffee prices and operating margins remain important variables.

10. Ingersoll-Rand India (Choice International)

MCap: ~₹12,500 Cr

A high-quality industrial compressor business with a strong profitability record. Manufacturing capex and demand for energy-efficient equipment support growth. The attraction here is business quality, although the stock is rarely available at a bargain valuation.

11. VA Tech Wabag (Mirae Asset Sharekhan, Monarch)

MCap: ~₹12,400 Cr

Water treatment and desalination remain important investment areas. Wabag has an established position in both. The bigger question is how efficiently the company executes projects and converts its order book into cash.

12. Gravita India (JM Financial)

MCap: ~₹10,900 Cr

Recycling is becoming a more organised industry, and Gravita has been expanding across materials and geographies. New capacities and better utilisation could support earnings. Cash flows and returns on fresh investments will be worth tracking.

13. Unimech Aerospace (Motilal Oswal)

MCap: ~₹8,900 Cr

Precision manufacturing for aerospace and specialised engineering. Motilal Oswal projects 75% revenue and 69% PAT CAGR during FY26–FY28. These are exceptional growth expectations, but such numbers also leave little room for execution delays.

14. RateGain Travel Technologies (Choice International)

MCap: ~₹8,600 Cr

An interesting software business serving hotels, airlines and travel companies globally. Recurring revenues and operating leverage could improve profitability. The recent correction makes it worth revisiting, provided earnings expectations remain intact.

15. Time Technoplast (Equirus)

MCap: ~₹8,400 Cr

Industrial packaging may not sound particularly exciting, but the company's move towards composite cylinders and other higher-value products could improve margins and return ratios. An interesting business mix story.

16. Genus Power (SBI Securities)

MCap: ~₹8,000 Cr

One of the direct beneficiaries of India's smart meter rollout. The opportunity is large, but the real test is how quickly orders convert into revenue and, more importantly, cash. Working capital deserves particular attention.

17. Kirloskar Pneumatic (Arihant Capital)

MCap: ~₹7,400 Cr

An established industrial engineering business in compressors and refrigeration. Demand from manufacturing, process industries and industrial investment could support growth without depending on a single end market.

18. Technocraft Industries (Equirus)

MCap: ~₹6,200 Cr

A relatively less-discussed manufacturing company with industrial products, precision engineering and textiles. The interesting part is whether the growing higher-value engineering businesses can improve overall margins and profitability.

19. HEG Advanced Materials (Arihant Capital)

MCap: ~₹5,700 Cr

Battery materials, advanced carbon technologies and energy storage make this an interesting long-term opportunity. The ambitions are sizeable, but much of the new business is still being built. Execution over the next few years will determine how much value is actually created.

20. TD Power Systems (PL Capital)

MCap: ~₹18,600 Cr

Industrial generators with exposure to global power and infrastructure investments. Demand from exports and power equipment offers opportunities. Following the recent correction, the important question is whether earnings growth can justify the valuation.

Concluding Remarks:

What I found interesting is how strongly engineering, precision manufacturing, electronics and industrial businesses feature across these brokerage recommendations. A few companies have the potential to grow earnings at 25–30% annually, perhaps even higher. Some may also offer asymmetric opportunities if new capacities, better margins or business diversification deliver more than what the market currently expects.

But valuations cannot be ignored, specially in some of the momentum picks here.
I would rather buy a company growing earnings at 20–25% at a reasonable to very slightly expensive valuation than pay very excessive price for 35–40% growth.

My next step is to narrow these 20 names further, looking at FY27–FY30 earnings, ROCE, cash flows, debt and, most importantly, what is already priced into the stock. I will share the final shortlist, along with my detailed analysis and preferred picks, with WealthEnrich subscribers.
For now, these are research candidates drawn from brokerage recommendations, not a final buy list.
Which 3-5 companies from these 20 would you consider the strongest opportunities for the next few years?

A former Minister of Environment, Mr. John Odey, has said former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi was instrumental to the creation of the Nigeria Erosion and Watershed Management Project (NEWMAP).

Odey spoke yesterday in Abuja at the official launch of the project at the Transcorps Hilton.

It was Thursday, November 5, 2009, at approximately 1:30 p.m. Amber was inside a processing center where soldiers were preparing for deployment. It had been an ordinary day until a gunman suddenly opened fire. Screams filled the building. People fell to the ground. Soldiers on the post were unarmed, and chaos erupted.

But Amber did not freeze. She ran toward the wounded. She tore up her blouse, fashioned a tourniquet, and tied it around an injured comrade to help stop the bleeding. She continued moving from one wounded person to another, refusing to stop and think about her own safety. She was so focused on helping others that she never realized a bullet had struck her in the back.

She discovered she had been shot only later, while receiving treatment in an emergency room. That evening, she called her mother, Lisa Pfund, who was relieved to hear from her daughter. Amber explained what had happened and told her that she hadn't even known she had been hit.

The November 5 attack claimed 13 lives and wounded 31 others, making it the deadliest mass shooting ever to take place on a U.S. military installation.

Amber survived.

Five days later, President Barack Obama visited Fort Hood, where approximately 5,000 people gathered for a memorial service. He shared the stories of those who had been killed and also recognized the courage of those who survived. Among them was Amber. He described how determined she had been to help others, explaining that she did not realize for some time that she had been shot in the back.

The following day, First Lady Michelle Obama also shared Amber's story. She had met the young soldier at Fort Hood, where Amber explained what mattered most to her: the safety of her fellow soldiers was her number one priority.

Years later, the Army announced that Purple Hearts would be awarded to victims of the Fort Hood attack. Amber was among those recognized for her wounds.
